name: Berthier, Prince de Neufchatel, to Napoleon (22 December 1812), "Chiffre du Prince de Neufchatel" -- "La Primata a ete dechiffree"
date: 22 December 1812 (retreat from Russia; Berthier chief of staff, letter location Koenigsberg per napoleon2.htm)
ciphertext: ciphers/berthier-napoleon-1812/ciphertext_full.tsv (LANE R6 Y9, 25 Sept 2026, two independent blind passes from the Vilcoq 1969 plate image, reconciled; use this file, not ciphertext.txt, which is Cryptiana's re-typed excerpt and has 10 of 325 groups differing from the image, logged in NOTES.md)
ciphertext_source: J. Vilcoq, "Le Chiffre sous le Premier Empire", Revue Historique des Armees no.4 (1969), pp.22-27, plate on p.24 (persee.fr doc/rharm_0035-3299_1969_num_25_4_8686, illustration renderIllustration/rharm_0035-3299_1969_num_25_4_T1_0024_0003_1.png), image-fetched and two-pass transcribed 25 Sept 2026 (LANE R6 Y9)
alphabet: numeric groups, no separators beyond whitespace, range 2-1388 (a nomenclator/large code, not letters-for-letters)
constraints: 325 groups total, 207 distinct, 136 hapax (66% of distinct codes occur once), commonest codes 918 and 13 (8x each), occupancy near-flat 1-1199 with few groups above 1200 -- this is the whole printed cryptogram (plate's last line is the visible end of the text, confirmed 25 Sept 2026), not a truncated excerpt of a longer one

Bourdeau's own structural read (dbourdeau/cyphersolver, napoleon/NOTES.md): a ~1200-entry nomenclator with 64% hapax at N=325 'is not a cipher that yields to analysis' from structure alone -- no cryptanalysis attempted on this basis (CLAUDE.md rule 3: a nomenclator this large at this N would fail its own matched control, so this spec's tests are lead tests, not a decode campaign)

no key found for this cipher in Cryptiana (sources/cryptiana/web/napoleon2.htm mentions a different, unnamed 'petit chiffre de l'armee' in a quoted letter, not a key table for the Prince de Neufchatel's cipher) or in Bourdeau's repository (grepped fresh 25 Sept 2026, no key file)

sender: Berthier (Prince de Neufchatel, major general of the Grande Armee); recipient: Napoleon; marginal note on the plate: 'Duplicata, Chiffre du Prince de Neufchatel, La Primata a ete dechiffree' -- so a contemporary decipherment (the 'Primata') likely exists in the archives but has not been located in print by this repo

Chuquet 1912 (archive.org 1812laguerrederu03chuquoft) prints Berthier's clear letters of the same December-1812 run as a possible crib source; his edition flags cipher letters explicitly elsewhere (VIII, 16 Dec, 'En chiffres.'; XI, 18 Dec, 'la note chiffree que j'ai adressee a Votre Majeste') but does not flag any single letter as the decipherment of this specific cryptogram
cheap_tests_in_order: 0. Crib fit: does any of Chuquet's 34 dated Dec-1812 Berthier-to-Napoleon clear letters (scripts/letters.json, LANE R6 Y9) fit the 325-group cryptogram as a plaintext, scored on 3 independent metrics (length fit, repeat-rate fit, repeat-gap-distribution fit) against a matched control of the other 33 letters in the same pool (scripts/crib_test.py). Disk-only, no fetch. Cost <$1.

1. Correspondance de Napoleon Ier vol. XXIV, 'votre note chiffree' lead (named by both Tomokiyo/Cryptiana napoleon2.htm and Bourdeau's napoleon/NOTES.md: Napoleon's letter to Berthier of 30 Dec 1812 acknowledges 'votre note chiffree' together with a letter of the 21st): find the letter on archive.org full text (correspondancede24napouoft) and read whether it quotes, answers, or otherwise identifies the content of the 22 Dec cipher. IA advancedsearch + be-api fts, <=20 requests, >=1.5s apart.

2. One-part vs two-part code test: do the code numbers of high-frequency French function words (if any crib from test 0/1 ever lands) ascend with alphabet order -- stated only, not run (needs a crib first).

3. William Urban's find of Berthier's cipher-use instructions in the Russian State Military Historical Archive (RGVIA), Moscow (named on Cryptiana's napoleon2.htm, 'Urban found ... but apparently not the code itself [Urban p.324]') -- a print lead naming a specific archive and author, not yet checked by anyone in this repo; needs identifying Urban's book/article and its full citation before it can be run as a test.
matched_control: test 0: the same 3-metric fit test run against all 33 other Chuquet Dec-1812 Berthier letters in scripts/letters.json (34 total incl. the two candidates named in the original brief, XIX and XXIII) -- a fit means something only if it beats this field on a majority of the 3 metrics (CLAUDE.md rule 3)

cheap_test_done.method: scripts/crib_test.py (already written by LANE R6 Y9, re-run this pass to extend its ranking table to letter XXIX, the single best length-fit letter in the pool, not one of the two candidates the original R6 brief scored on rate/gap) -- disk-only, ciphers/berthier-napoleon-1812/scripts/letters.json and ciphertext_full.tsv
cheap_test_done.target: letter XXIX (28 Dec 1812, 316 words) ranks 1st of 34 on length_fit (0.0277, best in the whole pool), 12th of 34 on rate_fit (0.0705), 17th of 34 on gap_fit (0.2737, just inside the top half)
cheap_test_done.control: the other 33 Chuquet Dec-1812 letters on the same 3 metrics -- median rank 17.5 of 34; XXIX beats the control median on all 3 metrics (1st, 12th, 17th are all <=17)
cheap_test_done.verdict: beats its control on a majority (in fact all three) of the metrics, unlike XIX (beats the control on only 1 of 3: rate_fit 3rd, but length_fit 15th and gap_fit 18th) and XXIII (never above the middle of the field on any metric: 18th, 29th, 30th) -- both scored by the prior LANE R6 pass. This is a length-fit-driven result, not a decode: length fit alone (325 groups vs 316 words, one code roughly per word) is a weak, easily-coincidental signal at N=34 candidates and 3 metrics, and rate_fit/gap_fit for XXIX are only mid-pack, not standout. Not a crib, not a claimed alignment -- a lead worth the print check in test 1 (does XXIX, or the 28 Dec date, appear in Napoleon's reply correspondence), not a cryptanalytic result (rule 4: no H/C grade, no S grade -- no alignment is proposed).

cheap_test_done.method: archive.org advancedsearch (1) confirmed correspondancede24napouoft is vol. XXIV; be-api fts (5 queries: "note chiffrée", "30 décembre", "lettre du 21", chiffrée, "lettre du 22", >=1.5s apart) plus one direct fetch+grep of the volume's full _djvu.txt (43,181 lines) since be-api's page_num field is a known-broken locator (CLAUDE.md Access playbook)
cheap_test_done.target: "note chiffrée" -- 0 hits anywhere in the volume (confirms CX2's prior negative). Nearest cipher-marked letter found (19275, Napoléon to Maret/Bassano, Moscou 16 Oct 1812, "lettre en chiffre") is a different correspondent and date, unrelated. Letter 19408 (Napoléon to Berthier/Prince de Neufchatel, Paris, 30 Dec 1812) is the closest match to the napoleon2.htm lead's shape (same addressee, same date, acknowledges a dated letter and a note) but its actual text reads "j'ai reçu votre lettre du 21 ; j'ai reçu aussi votre note pertes réelles" -- the 21st, not the 22nd (this target's date), and "note pertes réelles" (real-losses report), not "note chiffrée" (ciphered note). "lettre du 22" (5 hits) matches none to Berthier or a cipher (Rapp/Danzig, Lauriston, unrelated business).
cheap_test_done.control: not applicable -- this is a print/archival lookup (rule 3's control requirement is for a claimed cryptanalytic or crib result; this is a search-and-read, reported per rule 2's 'every difference' standard against the secondary-source paraphrase, not gated against a random draw)
cheap_test_done.verdict: not found as claimed: the 30 Dec 1812 letter to Berthier (19408) exists and is real, but its wording does not match napoleon2.htm's paraphrased 'votre note chiffrée' (says 'note pertes réelles' instead) and answers a letter of the 21st, not the 22nd. Either the secondary source's paraphrase names the wrong note, or a different letter/note this pass did not locate is meant. Not resolved either way; reported as a discrepancy, not a refutation or a confirmation.

judge.note: fr18 (diplomatic/official French prose, c.1680-1790) is the only French corpus tools/judge_plaintext.py actually wires besides the default fr16 (16th-c. letters); fr19 (French prose 1800-1890, tools/data/fr19/) exists on disk but is NOT in LANG_CORPORA as of 25 Sept 2026, so a spec cannot opt into it yet. fr18 is a 22-132-year era mismatch (target is Dec 1812) and fr16 is a ~230-year mismatch; fr18 is picked as the closer of the two wired options, but per CLAUDE.md's era-corpus lesson (V6-PTCORP) any judge PASS/FAIL against fr18 on this target should be treated as unreliable until a French corpus of Napoleonic-era official/military prose (1800-1815) is built and wired -- flagged here as a one-line suggestion, not built this pass (out of a $3 breadth cap).

value: low as a solver target at N=325 against a ~1200-entry nomenclator (Bourdeau's own structural objection, CLAUDE.md rule 3 ladder would fail its control) -- the live leads here are all print/archival (a contemporary decipherment likely exists per the plate's own marginal note), not cryptanalytic; kept on the breadth list for its lead tests, not for a future campaign cap above $10 without a new formal constraint (a located key or a confirmed crib)
